summary: TechCrunch explains why the Supreme Court agreed to hear challenges to Florida and Texas laws restricting how social media companies moderate content. Drawing on NYU's Paul Barrett, it covers the circuit split that brought the cases up, the First Amendment question of platforms' editorial judgment, how the two laws differ, and the possible consequences for platforms and users.
one_line: The Supreme Court will decide whether Florida and Texas laws limiting social media content moderation violate platforms' First Amendment right to editorial judgment.
key_facts: The Supreme Court agreed to hear a pair of cases over Florida and Texas state laws restricting how social media companies moderate content.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis signed Senate Bill 7072 into law in May 2021.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott signed House Bill 20 in September 2021.
NetChoice and the Computer and Communications Industry Association (CCIA) challenged both laws, and federal trial judges entered injunctions blocking them on constitutional grounds.
The Eleventh Circuit (Florida) and the Fifth Circuit (Texas) clashed, and this explicit conflict is one basis the Supreme Court uses for taking cases.

The core question is whether social media companies have a First Amendment protected right to exercise editorial judgment, or content moderation, on platforms they own; the case concerns the companies' rights, not users' rights.
Texas HB 20 bars platforms from removing or demonetizing content based on the 'viewpoint represented in the user's expression.'
Florida SB 7072 would stop platforms from banning political candidates or removing or restricting their content.
Republicans have accused social media companies of suppressing conservative viewpoints since the early Trump administration, though research has not supported these claims.
Senator Ron Wyden, co-author of Section 230, said a ruling in favor of the laws would create 'utter chaos' and make many sites worthless to regular users.
NetChoice President Steve DelBianco warned the laws would unleash 'a tidal wave of offensive content and hate speech.'
The laws also require individualized explanations when content is removed; Paul Barrett said this would be onerous given that millions of pieces of content are taken down daily, mostly automatically.
